_note: Sequenced curriculum. Body text supports [[entry-id]] links into encyclopedia.json, which open as definition cards in place. Lessons are meant to be read in order; each course states what it assumes.

courses.title: Start here
courses.summary: The question under test, the analogy behind it, and how to work with the instrument.

lessons.title: The question
lessons.body:
A sound that crosses from left to right is heard at one position and then at another, and the sequence is perceived as movement. That much is well understood.

The question here is whether a whole [[field]] of sound can be heard as moving when nothing inside it can be singled out and pointed at. Motion is a global property of the field, and localizability is a local property of its parts, so the two can be set independently and varied against each other. The claim under test is that the first survives the removal of the second.

The standard account of [[auditory-motion]] holds that motion is inferred by comparing successive position estimates. On that account a field with nothing localizable in it supplies no estimates to compare, and should not be heard as moving. A listener who hears motion anyway would show the account to be incomplete.

Motion is meant broadly throughout. A field can turn about the listener, close in or open out, or drift past in a straight line, and the instrument builds all of these from the same parts. Rotation was the first case examined and is the easiest to describe, which is why it recurs in the examples, although nothing in the question depends on it.

Listening sessions always address two things: whether anything in the field can be pointed at, and whether the field is moving.

lessons.title: The analogy that motivates it
lessons.body:
In vision the corresponding question is partly settled. A [[random-dot-kinematogram]] is a field of dots in which some proportion move in a common direction while the rest move at random. Observers report the global direction well below the proportion at which any single dot can be followed, so the motion is computed by pooling across elements and belongs to the ensemble; see [[global-motion]].

That result is why this project treats motion as something an ensemble might carry rather than as something read off a tracked object. It is established vision science with an identified neural substrate.

The analogy reaches less far than it first appears. Every dot in a kinematogram stays visible and localizable throughout, and the manipulation varies how many dots share a direction rather than whether a dot has a position. The paradigm therefore speaks to pooling and stays silent on motion perceived without localization, since that condition never arises in it.

This instrument varies two things where the kinematogram varies one. The [[motion-coherence|motion coherence share]] carries the kinematogram manipulation over directly, and the parallel there is close. [[decorrelation|Decorrelation]] is the second, and it has no visual counterpart: it removes each source's position rather than its informativeness about direction. The question this project exists for turns on that second manipulation.

A structural limit applies to both. Vision resolves many independent spatial channels while hearing reconstructs space from a comparison between two ear signals, so any auditory pooling would operate on [[interaural-statistics|interaural statistics]] rather than on a spatial map.

lessons.title: What the instrument does
lessons.body:
The instrument sums a piece of audio to mono and builds a [[field]] from it: virtual [[source|sources]] placed around the head, each filtered to differ from the others, each given an angle and a [[source-distance|distance]] through a head model.

Work is organised in three levels. A [[passage]] is a time region of the track. A [[variant]] is one treatment of that passage, or the untreated signal. A [[component]] is a lattice of sources with a motion applied, and a variant is built from as many components as it needs.

Rendering produces every variant of a passage over the same span, sample aligned and matched in loudness, so a comparison between them isolates the treatment.

During playback the track runs untreated while each rendered variant runs alongside it in step. Holding a number key brings one forward and releasing returns to the untreated signal, with the change occurring mid-note.
lessons.try: A new passage starts with the untreated signal only. Add a variant, then add a component to it from the menu.

lessons.title: Working method
lessons.body:
Comparison is more sensitive the closer together the compared sounds are in time, because memory for spatial quality fades quickly; see [[auditory-memory]]. Switching between aligned variants in the middle of a sustained note is therefore a stronger test than listening to renders in sequence.

A workable loop: choose a passage of fifteen to thirty seconds, build two or three variants that differ in one parameter, render, loop the passage, and switch between variants repeatedly.

Three habits protect the conclusions. Change one parameter per comparison, since a difference heard between variants that differ in two ways cannot be attributed to either. Compare against the right reference, which for a moving field is the same field held still; see [[matched-control]]. Record what was heard before reading the measurements.

Listen on headphones, with any operating-system spatializer disabled, since those apply a second head model on top of this one.
lessons.try: With Loop passage on, press Play, then hold and release key 1 several times.

courses.title: How we hear direction
courses.summary: The two interaural differences, the cues they support, and where they fail.

lessons.title: Two ears, two differences
lessons.body:
The ears sit on opposite sides of the head, and this produces two measurable differences between the [[waveform|signals]] at the two eardrums. A sound to the right arrives at the right ear earlier, which is the [[itd|interaural time difference]], at most roughly 0.65 ms for a human head. It also arrives louder, because the head shadows the far ear, which is the [[ild|interaural level difference]].

Both differences are zero for directions on the [[median-plane]], the vertical plane of symmetry through the head, and maximal on the [[interaural-axis]] through the ears. What the pair really encodes is the angle from that axis, a fact with consequences covered later in this course.

Hearing that rests on comparing the two ear signals is called [[binaural]].

lessons.title: Timing and its limits
lessons.body:
A sound reaching the two ears is one pressure wave arriving twice, offset in time. Recovering that offset means working out how far one [[waveform]] has to slide before it lines up with the other.

The auditory system does this on the [[fine-structure|fine structure]] of the sound, meaning the individual pressure swings of the wave rather than its slower overall shape. Hair cells in the inner ear fire in step with those swings, at roughly the same point in each cycle, which is called [[phase-locking|phase locking]]. A nerve fibre driven from the left ear and one driven from the right then carry the offset directly, as a difference between the times at which they fire, and the brainstem compares them.

Two things end that arrangement above roughly 1.5 kHz. Phase locking itself degrades, since a cell cannot mark a cycle lasting a fraction of a millisecond precisely enough to be useful. And the [[wavelength]] falls below the width of the head, so more than one delay fits what the ears observe: a delay of one cycle looks identical to a delay of two, and the answer stops being unique.

Timing remains available above that range from the [[envelope]], the slower rise and fall of the sound's overall size, which stays unambiguous because it varies far more slowly than the wave inside it. Fine structure carries interaural timing at low frequencies and the envelope carries it at high ones.

How precise a renderer has to be follows from the human figure. Listeners resolve interaural delays of around 10 microseconds. Digital audio stores a signal as a list of numbers measured at regular instants, each one a sample; at the [[sample-rate|44.1 kHz]] used here, one sample covers about 23 microseconds, so the grid is more than twice as coarse as the smallest difference a listener can hear. Rounding a delay to a whole number of samples would therefore be audible, as an image that sits wrong or steps as it moves. Delays are placed between samples instead, by [[interpolation]]; see [[sampling]] and [[fractional-delay]].

lessons.title: Level and frequency
lessons.body:
The head shadows sound only when the [[wavelength]] is small relative to the head. A 100 Hz tone, with a wavelength near 3.4 m, bends around it by [[diffraction]]; an 8 kHz tone, with a wavelength near 4 cm, is blocked.

The [[ild]] is therefore a function of [[frequency]]. Measured from this instrument's model at 90° to the right: about +1.3 [[decibel|dB]] at 200 to 500 Hz, +7.8 dB at 1 to 2 kHz, and +15.2 dB at 4 to 8 kHz. A plausible head-shadow model is consequently a filter rather than a flat gain; see [[brown-duda-shadow]].

Together with the previous lesson this gives the [[duplex-theory]]: timing dominates at low frequencies and level at high ones.

One consequence recurs later. The bass carries very little level difference, so low frequencies offer almost no cue for position, and decorrelating them tends to produce vagueness rather than width; see [[bass-coherence]].
lessons.try: A variant's Decorrelation group carries crossovers and band amounts, which are there so the bass can be held coherent while the bands above it are decorrelated.

lessons.title: The cone of confusion
lessons.body:
Since [[itd]] and [[ild]] encode the angle from the [[interaural-axis]], every direction on a cone around that axis produces the same pair of values; see [[cone-of-confusion]]. Front and back at mirror-image angles are the simplest such pair.

Listeners resolve the ambiguity in two ways. The [[pinna]] imposes direction-dependent [[spectral-cues]], mostly above 5 kHz, which differ between front and back and also carry [[elevation]]. More decisively, small head movements shift the cues in opposite directions for front and back sources; see [[head-movement-cue]]. Static headphone listening removes head movement, and the spherical model used here has no pinna.

The consequence for this instrument is complete [[front-back-confusion]]: azimuths 0° and 180° produce identical signals. A full rotation yields an interaural pattern that repeats twice per lap, so rotation cannot be distinguished from side-to-side oscillation at twice the rate, and rotation direction cannot be recovered. Listening questions about pointing remain valid; questions about direction do not, which is why the blind test does not ask one.

lessons.title: The spherical model's scope
lessons.body:
The head model is a rigid sphere of radius 8.75 cm; see [[spherical-head-model]]. From that geometry the [[woodworth-model]] yields the ITD and the [[brown-duda-shadow]] filter yields a frequency-dependent ILD, and both have been verified against the figures earlier in this course.

A sphere has no pinna, so the model produces no [[spectral-cues]], no [[elevation]], and no front-back discrimination, and it corresponds to no listener in particular; see [[individualization]]. It places sounds convincingly left and right and supports the [[coherence]] manipulations this project depends on.

The upgrade path is measured data in [[sofa]] format, for which the code already has a drop-in class. The substantive work there is [[hrtf-interpolation]], since naive blending between measured directions causes [[comb-filtering]].
lessons.try: [[head-radius|Head radius]] and [[speed-of-sound|speed of sound]] appear in a variant's Physical model group and feed the formulas above directly.

courses.title: Building a virtual field
courses.summary: Convolution, head-related filters, lattice geometry, and rendering a field that changes over time.

lessons.title: Impulse responses and convolution
lessons.body:
For a system that is linear and does not change over time, the response to a single instantaneous impulse characterises the system completely: the output for any input follows from it. That recording is the [[impulse-response]], and the operation that applies it is [[convolution]], in which every output [[sampling|sample]] is a weighted sum of recent input samples with the impulse response supplying the weights.

Most of this instrument is expressed in impulse responses. The path from a direction to an eardrum is one, and each decorrelating filter is one.

Direct convolution costs the product of the two lengths, so in practice both signals are transformed to the [[frequency]] domain, multiplied, and transformed back, which is one reason the renderer works in blocks.

lessons.title: A direction as a filter
lessons.body:
The delay, shadowing, and spectral shaping a direction imposes can be collected into one filter per ear, the [[hrtf]], or in the time domain the [[hrir]]. Convolving a mono signal with a direction's pair places it in that direction over headphones.

This instrument synthesizes each pair from the model: a [[fractional-delay]] carries the [[itd]] and the [[brown-duda-shadow]] filter carries the [[ild]]. Pairs are computed for each degree of [[azimuth]] and stored. Measured data in [[sofa]] format uses the same interface, so nothing downstream changes when it is substituted.

One implementation detail is audible if done wrongly: the delay filter's window must be centred on the delay rather than on the middle of the array, since the asymmetric truncation otherwise removes high frequencies; see [[windowed-sinc]].

lessons.title: Lattices of sources
lessons.body:
A field is built by repeating the single-source operation: take the mono signal, make several versions of it, place each at its own [[azimuth]] and distance, and add the results.

Sources are placed by a **lattice**, of which there are two. A [[polar-lattice]] is concentric rings, so many rings across a radial band with so many sources around each. A [[grid-lattice]] is a rectangle of sources spanning an extent in metres. One ring at a single radius is the simplest polar case and is where this project began.

Geometry interacts with symmetry. In an even ring every source has one directly opposite, and opposite pairs of identical signals cancel each other's interaural contributions; see [[antipodal-cancellation]]. Odd counts avoid exact opposition, and staggering successive rings stops them lining up on shared spokes.

A lattice on its own is static. The same lattice can be turned, drawn inward, or carried past the listener without any change to how its sources are placed, which is why placement and motion are separate settings.

Identical copies on a symmetric lattice cancel completely, a result taken up in the course on coherence.
lessons.try: In a component, compare 4 evenly spaced sources against 5, then raise the ring count to 3 and watch the monitor.

lessons.title: Rendering a moving field
lessons.body:
A moving source requires a filter that changes over time, and an abrupt filter change produces a click. The renderer therefore processes short overlapping blocks, convolving each with the [[hrir]] for the angle at the block's midpoint and summing the results; see [[overlap-add]].

Blocks are tapered by a [[window-function]] that doubles as the crossfade between successive filter settings. The taper must satisfy [[cola]], the condition that overlapping windows sum to a constant, since otherwise the output rises and falls in [[amplitude]] at the block rate. A periodic [[hann-window]] at half-block overlap satisfies it exactly.

The default block of 256 samples updates every position about 344 times per second, far beyond what the binaural system can follow; see [[binaural-sluggishness]]. Motion is therefore continuous as far as a listener is concerned, and the block length is chosen for the cost of the transform rather than for the smoothness of the trajectory.

The same per-block schedule updates the filters that make sources differ from one another, so a field can change its internal structure while it moves. Those filters are the subject of the next course.

courses.title: Coherence and decorrelation
courses.summary: Why identical copies cancel, how copies are made to differ, and what each control contributes.

lessons.title: Two coherences
lessons.body:
Two signals are coherent when one predicts the other, and incoherent when it does not, with a continuum between; see [[coherence]]. The measure used is the [[correlation-coefficient]], which is normalised so that level does not affect it.

Two distinct coherences appear throughout this instrument. Inter-source coherence holds between source signals before spatialization, is what the decorrelation controls act on, and is reported as a [[coherence-matrix]]. Interaural coherence holds between the two ear signals after summation and is measured as [[iacc]]. The two are related but move separately, and conclusions drawn about one from the other are unreliable.

lessons.title: The degenerate ring
lessons.body:
An evenly spaced ring whose sources all carry the same signal renders with the left and right channels identical to machine precision. The result is a centred mono image with no interaural information, and moving it changes nothing beyond a faint timbral shimmer from shifting [[comb-filtering]]. The measurement appears in the test suite; see [[degenerate-ring]].

The cancellation is a symmetry property: summing identical copies over a symmetric arrangement removes exactly the interaural differences that would carry direction. Motion of any kind can only be audible after the symmetry is broken, through [[decorrelation]], uneven spacing, per-source gain, or per-source coherence; see [[symmetry-breaking]].

A silent-seeming result is most often this configuration, so it is the first thing to check.
lessons.try: Add a Ring, which places six sources evenly at two metres, and set the variant's [[decorrelation-amount|decorrelation amount]] to zero. Measured IACC is 1.000. Raise the amount and watch it fall.

lessons.title: Decorrelating without changing timbre
lessons.body:
The requirement is copies that are mutually incoherent while each still sounds like the original. [[timbre|Timbre]] follows the [[magnitude-spectrum]], so the filters must leave magnitude essentially flat while altering timing, which is the definition of [[allpass-filter|allpass]].

Two constructions are used. A random-[[phase]] allpass filter scrambles the [[phase-spectrum]] completely and preserves magnitude exactly, at the cost of smearing [[transient|transients]]. [[velvet-noise]] places sparse random-sign impulses on a jittered grid, is nearly colourless, cheap to convolve, and gentler on transients.

The two lie on one axis: as velvet's [[impulse-density]] rises, the sequence approaches a random sign sequence, which is the allpass case. The blend between the untreated and filtered signal is the [[decorrelation-amount]].

lessons.title: Which controls do work
lessons.body:
Measured on this system, the controls differ widely in usable range.

[[ir-length|IR length]] has the most: inter-source coherence runs from about 0.19 at 5 ms to 0.04 at 120 ms, large against the measurement [[noise-floor]] of roughly 0.05. Longer filters also smear transients more.

[[impulse-density|Density]] acts only while the filter is sparse, with coherence falling from about 0.50 at 60 impulses per second to 0.07 at 400 and remaining flat beyond; see [[density-saturation]].

[[ir-envelope|Envelope]] dominates in the sparse regime and is nearly inert once dense, and it previously [[confound|confounded]] comparisons between the two filter families; see [[envelope-confound]]. It is held fixed when anything else is compared.

[[phase-depth|Phase depth]] provides a smooth route to partial coherence. [[micro-delay]] and [[micro-pitch]] decorrelate crudely and colour recognisably, and are kept for comparison. The [[coherence-lfo]] varies the amount over time.
lessons.try: Set envelope to flat explicitly and sweep IR length from 5 to 120 ms across renders, watching the measured coherence.

lessons.title: Level and the low end
lessons.body:
A plain blend between the untreated and filtered signal is not power preserving: the components partially cancel, and the middle of the sweep sits several [[decibel|decibels]] below the ends. Loudness differences dominate subjective comparison, so such a control would make every comparison about level. Each control here holds per-source level constant through a closed-form correction, verified per control in the test suite; see [[level-preserved]] and [[level-matching]].

[[frequency|Frequency]] receives separate treatment. The bass carries little [[ild]], so decorrelating it produces vagueness and risks partial cancellation on summing, and common practice keeps it coherent; see [[bass-coherence]]. The [[crossover]] is adjustable because that practice has not been tested on rotating fields, and the band splitting is arranged so that uniform band amounts change nothing at all.

courses.title: Putting a field in motion
courses.summary: Building motion from a lattice and a velocity: turning, closing in, drifting past, and mixtures of the three.

lessons.title: Motion in unison
lessons.body:
The main configuration is a group of mutually decorrelated sources moving together, which this project calls [[unison-motion]].

Its two properties come from two independent controls. The component's velocity moves every source together and keeps the formation rigid. The [[decorrelation-amount]] removes each source's individual locatability. At low decorrelation the result is trackable objects moving around the listener, which is unremarkable; at high decorrelation the sources merge into a diffuse field, and whether that field is still heard to move is the experimental question.

The motion itself is open. Rotation turns the lattice about the head, [[radial-flow]] draws it inward or outward, and [[translation]] carries it past the listener in a straight line. These combine within a single [[component]], so a [[whirlpool]] is one polar lattice turning while flowing inward, with its inner rings set to outrun the outer ones.

The design point holds across all of them. Decorrelation is what makes the field unlocalizable, and the velocity is what makes it move, and keeping the two separate is what makes the question testable.
lessons.try: The monitor shows this directly. Each source drags a trail, and the outline connecting a ring turns without changing shape while its sources move together.

lessons.title: Choosing rates
lessons.body:
Every motion has a usable band. It is bounded below by too little change to register within a listening window, and above by the binaural system's own inertia.

For rotation the lower bound comes from the [[mama|minimum audible movement angle]], and the upper bound from [[binaural-sluggishness]], an integration window of a hundred milliseconds or more that smooths quickly changing cues into texture. Working figures from listening here: a slow drift near 30°/s, clear rotation between roughly 60 and 120°/s, and loss of the motion impression somewhere past a few hundred. The turning presets sit at 60°/s, and the whirlpool runs its inner ring at 160°/s against 40°/s at the outside.

Radial flow and translation are set in metres per second, and their usable range depends on the size of the lattice as well as the speed. Translation sweeps azimuth quickly when the lattice is close and slowly when it is far, so a wide lattice tolerates more speed than a narrow one; the drifting presets run between 1 and 2 m/s across an extent of eight to ten metres. Radial flow changes level and near-field balance rather than angle, and reads clearly at lower speeds, with the closing and opening presets at 0.8 m/s across a band from 0.8 to 6 metres.

One point applies to rotation alone. Front-back symmetry in this model makes the interaural pattern repeat twice per lap, so a ring turning at 90°/s modulates the cues at 0.5 Hz; see [[interaural-pattern-rate]]. Translation and radial flow have no equivalent fixed rate, which matters when the measures are introduced later.

lessons.title: Choosing material
lessons.body:
Material affects the outcome more than any parameter. Under identical treatment, sustained theremin passages reach [[iacc]] near 0.04 while guitar remains between 0.38 and 0.62; see [[transient-material]].

A [[transient]] is a sharp, precisely timed event, and such events give the auditory system discrete snapshots from which positions are fixed. Those snapshots are the [[localization]] the experiment is trying to remove, so material full of onsets works against the treatment regardless of settings.

Suitable material is sustained and nearly transient-free: pads, drones, bowed strings, organ, held voice, cymbal wash. When the percept fails to appear, the passage is worth changing before the parameters.
lessons.try: Treat a sustained section and a percussive section with identical settings and compare.

lessons.title: Depth, drift, and partial coherence
lessons.body:
Three further axes, all available on either lattice.

**Distance.** Each component sits at a distance in metres, carried by level and by the near-field growth of the [[ild]]; see [[source-distance]]. Two components at different distances make a field with depth, an inner and outer structure that can move together, at different speeds, or in opposite directions. Without reverberation the distance cue is thin, so expectations should be modest, though the level balance still separates them audibly. Distance may reach zero, where both ears are equidistant and the source is heard as a centred, in-head image.

**Translation.** A [[grid-lattice]] with a drift velocity carries the whole lattice past the listener, wrapping so the field is endless. The motivating image is moving through a space with sources at regular intervals. Left-and-right travel moves both interaural cues strongly while front-and-back travel moves neither, so travel toward and away is heard through level alone; see [[front-back-measured]].

**Partial coherence.** A share of any component's sources can be excluded from its motion, wandering instead with no net direction; see [[motion-coherence]]. This is the kinematogram's central manipulation: in vision the proportion of coherently moving dots sets the strength of the global motion signal, and the threshold on that proportion is a standard measure. Sweeping the share asks how much coherent motion the auditory ensemble needs before it reads as moving.

Wander counts as motion, so the matched control for any of these freezes the component rather than removing its rates, which preserves the spatial and level distribution exactly.
lessons.try: Add a grid drifting forward, then a second component with a high random share, and compare each against its own frozen control.

courses.title: Measuring, and testing honestly
courses.summary: What the measures show, how far they can be trusted, why motion cannot be read from a single render, and blind procedure.

lessons.title: IACC and its variants
lessons.body:
[[iacc]] is the correlation between the two ear signals at the best small time lag. Values near 1 indicate a coherent, centred image and values near 0 a diffuse one. The measure comes from room acoustics, where low values accompany [[envelopment]] and [[apparent-source-width|width]].

On a static ring it tracks the decorrelation amount monotonically, from 1.000 through roughly 0.92 and 0.55 to near 0.22 at full decorrelation.

Two refinements are reported alongside it. [[octave-bands|Per-band]] values show where the coherence went, with the low bands being where decorrelation costs the most. The [[iacc-over-time]] series shows change within a passage, which a single number averages away.

The next two lessons cover the measure's limits, which matter more than its values.

lessons.title: The noise floor
lessons.body:
The decorrelating filters are random draws, so identical settings measure differently under different [[seed|seeds]]. Across twelve seeds at full decorrelation, [[iacc]] has a standard deviation near 0.038, a measure of how far single draws sit from their own average, and spans 0.166 to 0.283, and inter-source coherence carries about 0.05 per draw; see [[noise-floor]].

Some effects under study are smaller than this. Ring geometry moves IACC by roughly 0.04 to 0.05, which single renders cannot resolve.

The working rules follow directly: hold the seed fixed when comparing two settings, average over seeds when characterising one, and treat any difference smaller than the floor as unresolved.

lessons.title: Motion needs a matched control
lessons.body:
[[iacc]] describes how diffuse a field is and cannot separate a moving field from a static one, since both can produce the same value. The alternative is to look for cyclic modulation of the [[iacc-over-time]] series at the [[interaural-pattern-rate]].

On music that measure is confounded by the material's own periodicity. Over a 20-second passage here, a completely static field scored a modulation ratio of 2.04 at 0.5 Hz while genuinely rotating fields scored 2.65 to 3.14, so the raw number cannot support a motion claim; see [[rotation-signature]].

The interpretable quantity is the difference against a [[matched-control]]: the identical configuration, same seed, frozen. The material's contribution then appears in both and subtracts out. The instrument pairs such controls automatically and reports the difference.

The paired figure stays noisy on short passages, having given +0.61 over 20 seconds and −0.91 over 12 for the same comparison, against a clean +4.74 on a synthetic drone with no competing periodicity. Long passages, synthetic sanity checks, and repetition across seeds are all warranted.

Only rotation has a well-defined cyclic rate to look for. Translation and radial flow recycle at a period set by the extent and the speed, and no modulation figure is reported for them, so they are judged by listening against a frozen control.

lessons.title: Disagreement between measure and ear
lessons.body:
The measures and the listening reports disagree in specific, repeatable ways. Velvet decorrelation measures slightly louder than allpass in [[lufs]] yet is reported quieter, with a much lower [[iacc]]. Ring geometry barely moves IACC in conditions where it may be plainly audible; see [[metric-vs-percept]].

These measures were developed for concert halls and steady sources and have not been validated on moving decorrelated fields, so the disagreements are informative about what the measures omit rather than errors in either direction.

The practice here is to record both, letting neither overrule the other, and to treat a heard difference that the measures deny as a result worth keeping once it survives blind testing.

lessons.title: Blind procedure
lessons.body:
The person who designed a stimulus knows what it should do, and that knowledge shapes perception below deliberate judgement; see [[experimenter-bias]]. The remedy is procedural rather than attitudinal.

A trial presents two conditions at once. The passage loops, one condition sounds while the space bar is held and the other while it is released, and the listener moves between them as often as they like before answering. This is the comparison the bench is built around, for the same reason: memory for spatial quality fades within seconds, so two renders heard in succession make a weaker test than moving between them; see [[auditory-memory]].

Four standard elements apply. [[blind-testing|Blinding]] hides which condition is which. [[randomization|Randomisation]] shuffles the order of the pairs and which side of the key each condition takes. [[forced-choice|Fixed response formats]] make answers countable with a defined chance level, and a free description is collected before them. [[catch-trial|Catch trials]] pair a condition with itself, where the correct answer is known exactly.

The bench serves unblinded exploration, and the blind test decides whether an explored difference is real; the two have different evidential standing.

Every result so far also comes from one listener who holds the hypothesis, on a non-individualized model; see [[n-of-1]]. Responses log to disk per trial with full parameters and export to CSV, so adding listeners requires no new construction.
lessons.try: The Blind test page runs on the selected passage's variants once they are rendered. Hold the space bar during a trial.
